body:
I'm not sure this is the best approach. Silently stopping the execution of scripts would probably lead to a lot of issues that are difficult to troubleshoot. I think the current implementation makes sense, having the release builds skip most runtime checks means small errors could still leave the script logic in a recoverable (or just partially functional) state.

In my opinion, this inconsistency could be better resolved by allowing users to also ignore runtime errors in debug builds. The checks should still happen just for the debug build to log the errors, but the behavior should be the same as the release build. This functionality already exists, with the `Ignore Error Breaks` button in the editor and the `--ignore-error-breaks` cli flag, but the GDS runtime doesn't treat this accordingly, stopping execution regardless of this setting. This could probably be fixed by making sure the VM instruction pointer is incremented before doing the runtime checks, and continuing to dispatch opcodes after treating an `OPCODE_BREAK` (while the end is not yet reached).

This isn't exactly a silent stop. Often we'll see an error like `ERROR` as in the example. But I agree that this info might not be enough. So adding `SCRIPT ERROR` to the output seems like a good solution, but it could impact to performance.

Agreed, we could solve it that way too. But in my opinion, errors should stop execution by default anyway. Otherwise, if not, it leads to negative effects and vulnerabilities. For example,

```gdscript
var is_good := await is_good_user() # ERROR, in example, can't connect to server, not found network manager, etc...
if is_good:
    give_user_my_card_creds()       # Something horrible :D
```

<details>
<summary>GDScript example with details</summary>

```gdscript
func _process(delta):
	if get_parent():
		get_parent().remove_child(self)
	horrible_example()

func horrible_example() -> void:
	var is_good := await is_good_user()
    print("Is good user? %s" % is_good)
	if is_good:
		give_user_my_card_creds()

func is_good_user() -> bool:
	await get_tree().process_frame
	return true

func give_user_my_card_creds() -> void:
	print("OH, NO! MY CARDS!!!")
```

## With stop:
```
ERROR: Parameter "data.tree" is null.
   at: get_tree (scene/main/node.h:549)
Is good user? false
```

## Without stop:
```
ERROR: Parameter "data.tree" is null.
   at: get_tree (scene/main/node.h:549)
Is good user? true
OH, NO! MY CARDS!!!
```

</details>

Sure, it's a synthetic example, but it shows the danger. The problem is worse because GDScript doesn't provide any tools for error catching (like exception handling in C#).

Actually, there's another issue, because an error only stop current call execution. So next case is possible anyway:

```gdscript
var is_bad := await is_bad_user()   # ERROR, in example, can't connect to server, not found network manager, etc...
                                    # ERROR stop is_bad_user() execution, but var is_bad = false by default
if not is_bad:
    give_user_my_card_creds()       # Something horrible :D
```

I completely agree that the runtime checks are useful and provide additional safety, but I don't think it's feasible to have all the debug runtime checks in release builds, the performance impact would not be worth it. Also note that some debug checks are implemented in places other than the GDScript VM (check out `OperatorEvaluatorShiftLeft::evaluate` for example), so achieving full consistency would require changes in many different places, including the core.

I think it comes down to the priorities of the language. It's specialized for games, so even though script execution speed isn't usually a bottleneck, performance compromises should have really good reasons to be introduced. It is also intended to be easy to use, the checks in debug builds are really helpful and consistency is also important for usability. You could make the argument that the safety/security of release builds is also important to make the language more approachable and reliable, but I don't think it justifies the performance impact of all the checks. In my opinion, the better compromise is having only minimal runtime checks in release builds, for catastrophic errors, and debug builds that have comprehensive checks for testing and also an option to have the execution match the release build as closely as possible.

I understand.

Overvall, I don't think the changes in PR will have a big performance impact. It's just one branch that most of the time won't be taken, CPU branch predictor should handle it fine. But I could be wrong, needs testing. 

Some operations already has this check. For example, https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/c0ebded926fcec84a72656f8ff6d7f87a20064c2/modules/gdscript/gdscript_vm.cpp#L1466-L1472

Anyway, for GDScript: "ease of use is considered more important than performance" (c) [docs](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/performance/cpu_optimization.html#gdscript). In my opinion, ignoring code errors is not about "easy of use", it's about performance only.

Oh, my point about performance was mostly about keeping _all_ of the debug runtime checks for the release builds. 

The problem that this PR addresses is inconsistency between the behavior of debug and release builds (I hope I didn't misunderstand something). This won't be solved by keeping just some of the checks, all of them need to be accounted for. This is about usability in the sense that troubleshooting behavior that is inconsistent between types of builds is really inconvenient, so the solution should ideally address all instances of this behavior differences. The argument I was trying to make is that making the releases behave _exactly_ like debug builds would cause too much of a performance impact, so the next best thing would be to allow the option to do the opposite, making debug builds behave like releases for the purpose of testing and troubleshooting.

I could definitely be wrong about this performance impact of always having all of the checks, but at least some of them seem pretty involved, I don't think branch prediction could negate all impact. In a general purpose interpreted language, this would certainly be worth it, and it could also include some error handling system to allow users to manage errors however they wish. But with GDScript being so specialized, I don't think the same logic applies.

In my opinion, the problem may be that users don't distinguish between fatal and less severe errors. They appear identical in the editor, and users don't always understand that they must debug and fix them before release, otherwise the behavior in release builds is undefined. Developers also have different mindsets: some strive to have zero errors and warnings in their code, while others can easily have hundreds of errors and ignore them as long as the behavior appears correct.

Perhaps having three diagnostic levels (WARNING, ERROR, and FATAL ERROR) instead of the current two might encourage users to take fatal errors more seriously.

The difference between ERROR and FATAL ERROR could be precisely that FATAL ERRORs can be excluded from release builds, leading to behavioral differences between debug and release builds. We could also prevent code execution from continuing after the debugger stops on a FATAL ERROR (note, however, that not all engine errors cause the debugger to stop).

> The problem is worse because GDScript doesn't provide any tools for error catching

See #96529 for a potential step towards that.

Having a `call_with_error` probably wouldn't necessarily tilt things in favor of either the debug or release behavior, since both can be problematic depending on the context, but it would let you be a bit more explicit about what happens in the case where you can't afford to have an error.

The difference between debug and release behavior is difficult to wrangle with. I iterate on the game in editor, and run playtests with the team in debug exports (to gain better insight into bugs encountered). And yet there are bugs that may happen in release mode that did not occur in debug mode. Consider the following routine:

```gdscript
while true:
    await get_tree().process_frame
    do_something()
```

If the node is removed from the tree, get_tree() will log an error and return null. In debug mode this surfaces as an error being spammed, but the game basically works anyway, despite the issue. In release mode _this is an infinite loop!_ A tight loop that will lock the game up entirely.

Also consider what I should do as a developer on an architecture level when providing for systems that are data-driven. For example, a system that needs context whenever running an ability for an entity in the game:

```gdscript
push_context(entity)
execute_ability(entity.ability)
pop_context(entity)
```

There is nothing I can do as a developer of this code to _ensure_ that `pop_context` is called. If someone writes a buggy ability, it blows up and takes down the controlling system above it with it, at least, in debug mode it will.

Perhaps even more important is how it affects critical sections when using threads:

```gdscript
mutex.lock()
do_something()
mutex.unlock()
```

How do I ensure the mutex is released even if there's a bug? I cannot. A bug is likely to end up causing a deadlock and ruining the player experience.

You could say _just don't ship bugs_, but it's much more realistic to _plan_ for bugs than to assume they are all stamped out. You contain the blast radius of bugs with appropriately written code, and this in turn helps you fix them, which is a critical component of operating a live service game, where there are updates pushed to players on a weekly or even daily basis.

I think it is important for the language to provide a way to have control over the behavior, _and_ for the behavior to be consistent across debug/release.

This isn't entirely true. If an error occurs, only the current function is terminated, not the entire call stack. So the specific code structure shown in your example will work correctly:

```gdscript
func push() -> void:
    print("push")

func action_with_error() -> void:
    var x: Variant = null
    x.method()

func pop() -> void:
    print("pop")

func _run() -> void:
    push()
    action_with_error()
    pop()
```

Prints:

```
push
ERROR: res://run.gd:12 - Invalid call. Nonexistent function 'method' in base 'Nil'.
pop
```

> There is nothing I can do as a developer of this code to _ensure_ that `pop_context` is called.

If you want to increase the execution guarantees for specific code, such as proper resource release and so on, in case of unexpected bugs in your code, you can take advantage of the fact that even in the event of an error, local variables are cleared upon function exit, which causes the destructors of `RefCounted` objects to be called. This is the [RAII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_acquisition_is_initialization) idiom (Resource acquisition is initialization).

```gdscript
class Finally:
    var _on_destroy: Callable

    func _init(on_destroy: Callable) -> void:
        _on_destroy = on_destroy

    func _notification(what: int) -> void:
        if what == NOTIFICATION_PREDELETE:
            _on_destroy.call()

func _run() -> void:
    print("push")
    var _finally := Finally.new(print.bind("pop"))

    var x: Variant = null
    x.method()
```

For example, `FileAccess` (which inherits `RefCounted`) uses similar semantics. When this object is destroyed, the file is automatically closed. I'm not sure whether you're required to call `unlock()` on a mutex, as the documentation isn't clear enough. But if necessary, you can create a `RefCounted` wrapper to safely work with mutexes.

Also very useful tidbit!

This helps as I have more control than I realized. I do however still think it's unfortunate that there's a fundamental difference between how code executes in release and debug, especially since I have no way of running in editor in release mode.

I was curious how it handles a return value in that case. It looks like you get whatever the default for the type is. 

```gdscript
func _run() -> void:
	print("push")
	var x: Variant = null
	var i := action_with_error()
	print("pop: ", i)

func push() -> void:
	print("push")

func action_with_error() -> int:
	var x: Variant = null
	@warning_ignore("unsafe_method_access")
	x.method()
	print("after")
	return 8
```

In debug mode:
```
push
<error>
pop: 0
```

In release mode:

```
push
<error>
after
pop: 8
```

The behavior of the game is going to vary potentially drastically in the two modes.

We could also prevent code execution from continuing after the debugger stops on a FATAL ERROR (note, however, that not all engine errors cause the debugger to stop).

I don't understand. Doesn't the issue say behaviour in exports should be same? If differences in exports are acceptable, what's discussion and issue about?

`FATAL ERROR` seems like already implemented. It's `SCRIPT ERROR` that occurs in `gdscript_vm.cpp` and stops code execution for debug builds.

Still unclear how we'll define fatal errors and when to stop execution. Examples show that the same error should sometimes stop and sometimes continue based on context. In my opinion, decision about continue execution should be up to developers. Because only they understand what their code does. For example, like exceptions in C#: developer can choose crash program or handle exception and continue execution. By default program still terminates on errors, which seems like more expected behaviour...
